What makes organisations successful?
An extract from a book by an expert on management
My belief is that most managers have a fundamental understanding of what He ar
organisations work. They just need to be reminded of it, and encouraged to laa i ae
understanding to their own work. For example, it is only common sense that emp oyee aT
more likely to be committed to a cause or mission if they have had a hand in shaping it. Ay
does not need research to prove it. Nor do you have to see the research to know that wor!
groups are likely to produce better results than the same individuals acting on their own.
Furthermore, teams of ‘all-stars’ are not always, or even often, the best teams. The egos get
in the way of the sharing. The film 7rue B/ue, based on the Oxford University rowing team,
was a vivid example of this. The team dumped its international oarsmen because of their
arrogant stubbornness, replaced them with the second crew, and went on to win the Boat
Race against Cambridge University. We all have different talents and personalities. Put the
right people with the right companions into a group and everything clicks; get it wrong, and
there can be chaos. That is only common sense, even if it is uncommon in practice.
Above all, workers know instinctively that there has to be trust if any organisation is going to
work; trust between those in the group, that they will do their best and won’t undermine
each other, as well as trust in their leaders. People implicitly understand that the trust
involved has to be earned and can’t be assumed, that it depends as much on who they are
as on what they do, that it is fragile and, once lost, can seldom be restored. They also know
that it is hard to rely on colleagues they don’t know, or whom they only contact
electronically. Elaborate research studies are not needed to demonstrate such a basic truth.
Yet organisations need to trust their staff instead of cluttering themselves up with rules,
checks and checkers. Too much time is spent in organisations making sure that what should
be happening is actually happening. If employees know what they have to do and are
competent to do it, they should be left alone to get on with it.
I often ask business executives to list the people they know well enough to be able to rely on
to do the right thing when they themselves are not around and trouble is brewing. They
seldom come up with more than twenty names. That suggests that, to be truly effective,
organisations should be designed around operational units of up to twenty people. On paper,
that looks wasteful, so organisations inevitably adapt the design, optimistically hoping that
the economic logic of scale will prevail over the psychological need for trust and human
intimacy, and that everyone will do their best to make the place work. They are then
surprised to be disappointed. It is a particular difficulty for large organisations, whose very
existence is often based on those economies of scale. Could organisations have both
intimacy and scale, then, for both are necessary? Can you combine big and small? The
answer is yes.
One of my other beliefs is that we don’t need to reinvent a theory of organisations. As more
and more organisations are dependent on the skills of their people, they are having to treat

those people, even those at the lower end of the organisation, as professionals, people wn
recognised skills and talent.
Go to the theatre, I say to my readers and listeners. Look first at the programme as you wait
for the curtain to rise. Everyone connected with the performance is listed, no matter how
small their contribution. People like to be recognised as individuals. Theatre companies don’t
talk of their actors as human resources — none of them would work for them if they did.
Look more closely at that programme. The word ‘manager’ is reserved for those in charge of
things, not people: the stage manager, the lighting manager. Nor are the names of these
managerial people in large type; that distinction goes to the people who are in direct
communication with the customer — the actors — and they are directed, not managed, by
someone who actually leaves once the play is under way. He or she trusts the cast to go it
alone and, as often as not, they improve on the production once the director departs. Trust
inspires. What's more, at the end of each performance they receive an expression of
appreciation from their audience — direct feedback from the people who matter. No waiting
for the annual performance appraisal.
The lessons are all there for those who care to look. In professional and service
organisations, it is the person who is in direct contact with the client who is most responsible
for the first and often lasting impressions that are formed of the organisation. That may be
the person in the call centre, the engineer who comes to repair the machine, the sales
assistant behind the counter, even the waiter at your table. Paradoxically, however, it is
often the people in front of the customer who are the worst paid. That does not make the
task of management easy. How believable is it for managers to claim that these people are
crucial to the business, when the pay packet tells a different story? In a token gesture
towards the importance of individuality, organisations try to compensate a little by requiring
such people to display their name on a badge, for example. It fools no one, neither the
worker nor the customer.
